text: Pedro Alonso López (born 5 October 1948 – disappeared 22 September 1999), also known as the Monster of the Andes, is a Colombian serial killer, child rapist, and fugitive who murdered a minimum of 110 people, mostly pre-teen girls, from 1978 to 1980. López claimed to have murdered over 300 people in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru. He is considered by many as one of the most prolific serial killers and rapists in history. Born in the Tolima Department, Colombia, as the seventh of thirteen children, López was the son of Benilda López de Castañeda, a laundry worker, and Midardo Reyes, a rancher who was murdered six months before López's birth in an ambush during La Violencia. Benilda stated that Midardo was a local leader of a self-protection group aligned with the Colombian Liberal Party, while later accounts describe him as a member of the Conservative Party. After his father's death, Benilda fled to her mother's home in El Espinal, where she remained bedridden under midwives' care until López's birth. López claimed a difficult childhood due to household violence and the absence of a father, describing his mother as a prostitute who "was only good for putting children into this world, each from different men," and stating he often saw her and his stepfather have sex in front of him. Childhood neighbors reported that his mother was strict and forbade him from playing with them, and his mother claimed that López expressed hatred for her early on, telling her he couldn't stand her as a young child. According to López, he was banished from the house at age eight after his mother caught him groping his sister, spending a year homeless in Tolima, during which he was raped by a man who lured him with false promises of shelter and food. His mother claimed he ran away on 5 April 1958 in rebellion, asserting he did not want to live with her. At age ten, López moved to Bogotá, where he joined a gang of street children for protection and began using basuco and cannabis to combat malnutrition; he was occasionally sexually assaulted. At age twelve, he was adopted by an American immigrant family but ran away the same year, claiming a male teacher at the orphan's school had sexually harassed him, though biographers note no such incident occurred and that he left due to a lack of trust in his adoptive family. In 1969, López was sentenced to seven years in prison for auto theft; two days after arriving at La Modelo prison, he was raped by four inmates, and instead of reporting the assault, he killed three of them with a makeshift knife over two weeks. The killings were considered self-defense by prison staff, but his sentence was extended by two years. After his release in 1978, López wandered through the northwestern region of South America, staying in Bogotá and traveling through Tolima, Huila, Cauca, and Nariño to enter Ecuador, then Peru, claiming to do migrant work in the Llanos near Venezuela. He claimed between 1978 and 1980 to have killed over 100 girls, mainly street children and those from indigenous tribes. Though unverifiable, it is known that he was briefly captured by indigenous Peruvians in the Ayacucho region after attempting to abduct a 9-year-old girl; they beat him for several hours, stripped him of his clothes, and buried him up to the neck in sand, with reports stating their intention was to kill him through live burial, though López later claimed they poured syrup on him to allow ants to eat him alive. An American missionary convinced them to release him and turn him over to police, who did not detain him and instead expelled him from the country. After deportation, López resumed his killing spree in Ecuador, and although authorities noticed an increase in missing young girls, they concluded the disappearances were likely due to human trafficking. On 5 May 1979, López met Hortensia Garcés Lozada in Ambato, gave her 100 sucres to follow her, and raped and killed her under a nearby bridge. On 14 December 1979, in his hometown of El Espinal, he raped and murdered Flor Alba Sánchez. Two other girls were murdered in El Espinal on 21 December 1979 and 3 January 1980; Sánchez was found 20 days later buried on municipal property alongside Blanca Bautista, both bearing signs of torture. Sánchez is the only Colombian victim for whom López was tried; other cases were lost in a fire at the El Espinal courthouse. On 10 January 1980, he abducted Ivanova Jácome at a parking lot in Totoras [de], a suburb of Ambato, raped and murdered her in a nearby shack, with her body discovered at Ambato's Plaza Urbina on 15 February. López frequently visited Plaza Urbina, claiming to be a street merchant, but was usually seen at market stalls manned by young girls, offering them 100 sucres to accompany him, typically claiming to need directions to a bus stop. He was easily identified by his tall stature, prominent nose, lack of upper front teeth, and a large scar on his right cheek. In early 1980, two vendors, Luz Marina Lozada and Marina Cuenca, declined his offer and informed merchants of his behavior. On 9 March 1980, López tried to abduct 9-year-old Carmen Lozada, but her cries alerted bystanders, and he fled. Carmen identified him as the man who had previously offered her sister Luz Marina money. The plaza's merchant board president, Carolina Román Poveda, ran to rally others, was ignored due to heavy business, followed López out of the market, caught him talking to another 9-year-old girl, and intervened as he led her to a secluded path, shouting he was going to sell the child. Bystanders initially believed López, who claimed ignorance and called Román crazy, but due to her insistence and her assertion that he had previously tried to kidnap two girls, the crowd convinced them to bring López back, shoving and punching him. Román's fellow merchants criticized her, but she demanded he be handed over to authorities. López was taken to a police station but released shortly after. In April 1980, flash flooding in the Ambato area uncovered the remains of four missing girls, whose bodies showed signs of strangulation, prompting police to reopen investigations and contributing to López's eventual arrest. Three days after the flood, López approached 12-year-old Marina (or María) Román Poveda at Plaza Rosa market, flirted with her, offered 100 sucres to show him around, and she refused. She told her mother, Carolina, of his advances, recognized him, screamed at him, and grabbed his arm. She told bystanders he had tried to abduct her daughter and was responsible for the recently discovered girls. Local merchants overpowered López and held him until police arrived. While in police custody, López initially refused to cooperate, choosing to remain silent. Eventually, he began confessing to police captain Pastor Córdova Gudino, who shared a cell with him for 27 days. López boasted he had murdered a hundred in Colombia, at least 110 in Ecuador, and "many more" in Peru. He described his modus operandi as luring victims away from public spaces with a trinket, money, candy, or a job offer, then raping and strangling them with his bare hands for about 15 minutes, embracing their corpses as "muñequitas" ("dollies") until they became cold, leaving them at the scene and later covering them up. He claimed to occasionally exhume bodies and have "tea parties" with them. When asked about his motive, López said: "I lost my innocence at age eight. So I decided to do the same to as many girls as I could." In a 1992 interview, he admitted killing solely for sexual pleasure, stating: "It's like eating chicken. Why have old chicken when you can have young chicken?" He emphasized that he found it important that victims stay conscious until their eyes lost their light, calling it a "divine moment" and "terribly exciting." Because police doubted the authenticity of his confession, López offered to direct authorities to sites where he had left victims. He led Ambato police and families to a canyon of the Ambato River, where officers found the body of Hortensia Garcés Lozada beneath a bridge, held down by rocks. Police had to lock López in a patrol car to prevent lynchings. While driving to a second location, López described how he lured Garcés away with pedestrians nearby, and police found a decomposing body in an empty house. He later recounted meeting the victim in central Ambato, convincing her to accompany him out of town by bus, walking her around for hours, and raping her for twelve hours before killing her. Officers maintained an amicable tone with López to ensure cooperation. He led investigators to several more sites, mostly along the highway from Ambato to Quito, and recalled many murders before refusing to talk further, claiming his "friendship" with police had been betrayed. Ultimately, the bodies of 53 girls, aged eight to thirteen, were found, several in a forest near Ambato. While 28 sites named by López yielded no remains, police attributed this to scavenging animals unearthing and scattering body parts. Given the discovery of the mass grave, his estimate of 110 murders in Ecuador was accepted as legitimate. Authorities did not charge him with the total of 350 confessed murders because most occurred outside Ecuador and it was considered too costly to hold additional trials in Colombia and Peru. In 1980, López's trial began in Ambato under judge José Roberto Cobos Moscoso, charged with 57 counts of murder. On 27 January 1981, he was found guilty of three murders and received a 16-year sentence, the maximum available in Ecuador at the time. López served his sentence at the Garcia Moreno prison near Quito, where he was frequently attacked by fellow inmates, leading to increased security. Throughout the 1990s, he was often interviewed by journalists and made contradictory statements. He bragged about the rush he felt during strangulation but at other times claimed he was only an accomplice to Jorge Patiño, stating he only helped Patiño bury bodies after being raped by him and that he later murdered Patiño with a knife in Durán. His projected release date was controversial, with numerous lawyers petitioning for extensions or additional convictions. He was released two years early, on 31 August 1994. In an interview before his release, López called himself "the man of the century" and said he was released for "good behavior." He was transported from Quito to Ibarra, where a judge ordered his deportation. Press and public were present at the court, and López shook hands with several people. After the deportation order was read, police seized him and took him to a different vehicle for transport to the Colombian border, driving for five hours until nightfall to avoid pursuers, as families of victims had placed bounties on him, the highest being $25,000. In Colombia, he was received by DAS officers but, lacking a warrant, was temporarily held at a hotel in Pasto, with his room under surveillance but the door left unlocked, though he did not attempt escape due to fear of vigilantes. After a week, an arrest warrant was issued from El Espinal over suspicion of over a dozen murders, though no official case had been filed. He was transported to El Espinal, but after a van was ambushed by an angry mob of 2,000 people, he was taken to Bogotá for a medical examination until the situation calmed. López pleaded with doctors to release him, but was returned to El Espinal, where Alba Sánchez had filed a complaint over the murder of her daughter, as the state of her body resembled that of the girls murdered in Ecuador. López was convicted of the murder of Flor Alba Sánchez, though a physician believed he had signs of psychosis, requiring psychological treatment. The diagnosis was challenged, and he was designated as having "unhealthy personality traits" rather than a mental disorder, and was sent to the psychiatric ward of La Modelo prison. He did not receive medication and was noted as an unremarkable patient, engaging in heavy exercise, reading, and watching television. He maintained a well-groomed appearance but was never interviewed by the Colombian press due to lack of interest. In February 1998, López was declared sane and released on bail equivalent to US$70, on the condition of periodic reporting and therapy appointments; he almost immediately absconded. Ecuador's press and AFP reported on several alleged sightings in Tulcán and Ibarra, and a supposed capture in Cuenca that ended in his escape, but these claims were never verified. Within the year, López visited his mother to ask for money, but after she rejected him due to her poverty, he took her mattress and chair, sold them on the street, and left. The last reported sighting of López was on 22 September 1999, when he visited the National Civil Registry in Bogotá to renew his citizenship card, using the identity of a 60-year-old man from Aipe named Israel Césped to bypass checkpoints. In 2002, Colombian National Police and Interpol issued warrants for his arrest over a murder resembling his modus operandi. The Interpol warrant was deactivated in 2005 based on a claim by the National Institute of Forensic Medicine that an abandoned corpse had been identified as López, accepted by the National Registry, but he remains a fugitive. López has also been named as a possible suspect in the 2012 killing of Andrea Marcela García Buitrago in Tunja, Colombia, due to similarities with his 1979 murder of Flor Alba Sánchez. The most commonly reported victim count of 110 (not including the three prisoners killed by López in Colombia) is cited.

The last reported sighting of López was on 22 September 1999, when he visited the National Civil Registry in Bogotá to renew his citizenship card, using the identity card of a 60-year-old man from Aipe named Israel Césped to bypass checkpoints. In 2002, Colombian National Police and Interpol issued warrants for his arrest over a murder resembling his modus operandi; the Interpol warrant was deactivated in 2005 based on a claim by the National Institute of Forensic Medicine that an abandoned corpse had been identified as López, a claim accepted by the National Registry, though he remains a fugitive. López has also been named as a possible suspect in the 2012 killing of Andrea Marcela García Buitrago in Tunja, Colombia, due to similarities with his 1979 murder of Flor Alba Sánchez. The most commonly reported victim count of 110 (excluding the three prisoners killed by López in 1969) comes from his admission to Ecuadorian authorities, who only pursued those he stated he killed within Ecuador. Police searches in "almost every province" recovered several remains around Ambato and Santo Domingo, as well as individual gravesites near villages in cantons including La Troncal, Tulcán, Quito, Azogues, Manta, and Salcedo; of the Ecuadorian victims, only 17 were identified. Although López stated he killed a hundred victims in Colombia, he only confirmed the murder of two children in El Espinal. There are no known records about the victims murdered in Peru. Colombian journalist Jairo Enrique Gómez Remolina was one of the first to write about Pedro López (pseudonymised as Pablo Alonso Lopera); he travelled through Colombia's Andean Region to speak with parents whose daughters had gone missing and confronted López during a 1981 prison interview. Gómez Remolina is credited with linking López to child disappearances and killings in El Espinal, Pasto, Neiva, La Plata, Popayán, and El Bordo, though these were not definitively proven. He also speculated that López was responsible for the murders of young boys committed by the unidentified Monster of the Mangones (López denied travelling through Cali) and those of teenage girls by the Sadist of El Charquito (later attributed to Daniel Camargo Barbosa), later writing about López's prison interactions with Camargo Barbosa. Gómez Remolina was killed in 1986 during the Pozzetto massacre, having sat directly next to the perpetrator, Campo Elías Delgado. In 1992, López was filmed and interviewed by American journalist Ronald Laytner of the National Examiner. While media interest outside of Latin America was initially low, he received more coverage in the years leading up to his release and disappearance, often being referenced as a comparison to newly discovered serial killers such as Luis Garavito and Harold Shipman. Editions of Guinness World Records up to 2005 credited López as the "most prolific serial killer," but the listing was removed in newer editions after complaints that it made a competition out of murder.
